This game was exactly what I wanted from a hacking sim. It looks good, it plays good, it makes me feel like I know my way around a command terminal. It's easy enough that you don't ever get super stuck, but tricky enough that when you do figure out a problem or draw a connection, you feel clever and observant. 
I'd say that I want 15 more hours of it, because I genuinely do, and I'm totally going to get the DLC and also play loads of Workshop extensions - but honestly, I think the developer made the right call for the game, lengthwise. By the end you've gotten all the tools available to you, you know how to use them, and you're good enough that even the hardest security systems have started to become a breeze. Ergo, padding it out longer would have just gotten boring, without the challenge or some kind of new elements to spice it up. It ends when it's supposed to, but it also has some solid replayability. There's a hidden storyline and a couple achievements I couldn't get on my first playthrough, and some of the aspects are actually randomized each playthrough, so it's never exactly the same every time. Not to mention that because it's pretty much text based, it's one of the few games that even the most garbage of laptops could probably run, making it an excellent lightweight travel game for someone like me, who has the most garbage of laptops. 

Conclusion: It's a niche game, but it fits into that niche beautifully.

Just like I recommend a HOTAS for anyone playing Elite Dangerous, I recommend a mechanical keyboard with clicky blue switches for anyone playing Hacknet. An IBM model M buckling spring keyboard would be fantastic too, but they're kind of difficult to get nowadays. Why am I making this recommendation? Because you use the keyboard a lot in this game and pressing buttons and having them audibly and physically click stimulates the pleasure centers of my reptilian brain.

As you can probably guess from the name; Hacknet is a game about hacking. In terms of realism this game lies around the midpoint between 80's cyber movies and actual hacking, though noticeably closer to the former. It's visually engaging, it has a healthy degree of flashiness, it has a great retro synth soundtrack, and it has solid, well-defined mechanics.

Let's talk about these mechanics.

The game has various missions that you have to complete. They almost universally can be simplified to: hack into systems and do something. Sounds simple, but often there are plenty of obstacles that prevent you from doing that directly. Every system has a certain number of ports that are configured for different protocols. In order to hack into the server, you need to open a certain number of those ports. To do that, you use a programs specific to the protocols of each port to open them. Once they're open, you run another program to gain admin access to the system. Sometimes you have to overload a proxy, sometimes you have to analyze and solve a firewall, sometimes you get traced and it puts a big red timer there, and sometimes you can't hack the system! It might be because you don't have the programs you need, it might be because the hack would require more open ports than the system even has, or it might because [DATA EXPUNGED]. In any case, you're gonna need a password to get into those. Don't worry, I'm sure some idiot left it lying around somewhere...

You control the game through the terminal for the most part. It handles like a simplified unix terminal, which means unix veterans will feel right at home and windows users... well, we don't use terminals much anyway so it's not like we have to get used to new syntax. Wait, don't get scared off! You can always type "help [page number]" and the game will show you the available commands. Not only that, but you can press Tab to autocomplete your commands. You'll get used to it really fast.

I highly recommend this game. It's incredibly fun. If your budget allows, get the DLC too.

Next day I couldnt remember the password that was given to me for CSEC organization.. and the invitation letter showed an old password which didnt work, ( I think the game told me to change it earlier or something),  so I began to play the "REAL" game of hacking HACKNET GAME SAVE FILES...   without actually changing anything or leaving traces of my surreptitious visit..  :)  more info below...

SPOILER:
[spoiler]Reading multiple steam reviews and googling, I discovered the WIN10 save file location was under Documents/My Games/Hacknet/Accounts/save_******

A great game that I didn't expect to enjoy as much as I have. The abstraction of more complex concepts into simple commands was a great plan and keeps the game from feeling like a chore. Also, there are plenty of hilarious notes and other little things tucked away everywhere that provide some life in what could have been a dull, dry world. Some may not find this game fun at all due to the abundance of typing and reading, but if you're into this kind of "nerdy" thing then you're most likely going to love it.

--
Graphics/UI - 9/10
There are times I wish the visuals weren't quite so cluttered. Occasionally it can be frustrating to use the network map. The overall aesthetic is great though and it is very clear that a lot of care was taken in designing every little aspect.
--
Music - 10/10
Feels like you're in a hacker movie.
--
Input - 8/10
Emulating all the functionality of a terminal is hard. I think this game does a pretty great job at including enough of the functionality to cover the basics along with providing some quality of life shortcuts. I've encountered a few bugs that I wouldn't expect from real world terminal input, but nothing so bad that it breaks the game. (Tip: Use the up arrow on your keyboard to quickly cycle through your last used commands)
--
Story/Writing - 10/10
There is a *lot* of content to be found besides the main story, most of which ends up being brief glimpses into other peoples' lives. All of it is very well written and cohesive. (Beware some may be considered NSFW)

Pros:

2. You never (mostly) are left in the dark about what to do next
3. You can be a "real" Hacker for once

Neutral:

1. I can imagine that the music is not for everyone
2. Way too simple and straight forward compared to Uplink
3. Limited Options (while in Uplink you can hack Banks to get money or even give it to someone else, destory/save lives by manipulating police entries and such)
4. Missing does insane minigames, from Uplink, to crack a Lan and the option to build your own computersetup 

In-Depth Review:

I don't know if people still know that gem of a game called "Uplink". It's from the Year 2001 and was one of the best science fiction games back then (still is, but didnt aged very well). Hacknet is just a modern version of "Uplink". But it's extremly simplified compared to it, which have it's pros and it's cons of being so ofc. While Hacknet never reaches that incredible Depth Uplink offered, it's still have a lot of great moments itself, mostly because of a good storyline you can follow.

Hacknet is basically a pure text-based game in a science fiction setting. You are hacking computers, databases and other stuff 100% of the time. You wont do anything else. Don't except to buy your own computerparts, or anything like that. Playtime is around 10-20 hours and more if you have the DLC. 

The game is pretty easy and very straight forward. I have the feeling the game is holding your hands for a bit too long. But when it finally let you loose, oh boy, the felling of power and control is just awesome. There so many secrets to discover and little hidden stuff to look out for, it keeps you occupied for a few hours. And the music (it varies, but sometimes it's psytrance-like music and you get the felling you are on a Goa-Party) is pushing you all the time. You really fell like a "Supa Hacka" at times.

If you like the basegame, check out the DLC "Labyrinths" as well, because it lets you loose right from the start. It offers a own storyline to follow, new features, executables and Themes. 

Overall Hacknet and it's DLC, surely is worth the money if you like text-based adventures, want to learn/relearn a few basic Linux/Dos commands on the way, looking for a new Uplink for years (like myself), or just want to be a "Supa Hacka" for once.

Truth be told, I was already a GNU/Linux user years ago but I relied too much on the desktop environment(cheers MATE). I am familiar with several basic commands for bash terminal but thanks to this game I'm more comfortable using the command line for GNU/Linux systems.

Now about the game...

You play as a newbie hacker and you will be contacted by a well known info-sec/developer anon whose alias is Bit. After the 14 day timeout, an automation script will initiate a few start up tips to get your hands dirty as a script kiddie hacker. The more you delve deeper throughout this digital cyberspace the darker the game gets. Prepare yourself for an interesting battle of white hats vs black hats.

Full disclosure: I didn't buy this game as something I wanted, but I got it thrown in in a humble bundle package. 

I decided to give it a go expecting a hacking game which would be shallow and quickly turn boring.

Oh boy was I wrong. Just so you know: this is one of those games I wish I could replay for the first time.The game has so much depth to it that I got lost in it on many occasions. It has a few riveting story lines and the hacking you do to get into systems is never just about breaking in, but more about investigating and looking for clues that in the end allow you to break in.

Without spoiling too much, one of the most emblematic missions exemplifying the previous statement is a mission in which you are tasked to help someone euthanize themselves. I'm not going to say anything more than that it involves a pacemaker, but you can see the complexity that ends up behind some of the latter missions. 

The beginning of the game is really more of a tutorial with a ramping up by gathering new hacking tools and by the end of the game, you can hack everything easily, but the road you'll take towards your goal is going to be a real puzzle. 

So I liked this very much for the story and the surprising turn into an excellent puzzle game.

I can't recommend it enough, especially for a small price. I'm off trying the DLC, seems like that one is also a little gem.

PS: there's one story arc you can completely miss if you're not paying attention! The game is much more about observation than hacking. You've been warning.
This game is about hacking.

The TL;DR on Hacknet is that this, (including or excluding it's DLC companion, Labyrinths, which is a sort of expansion pack) is a beautiful, self-contained little experience that an average gamer can knock out in a day or two whether or not that gamer has the DLC, which revolves around themes of death, privacy, freedom, security, and compromise, all within the conceit of a terminal-interface hacking simulator. 

I don't want to spoil all that much, frankly, but there's an amazing array of moments, missions, results of your actions, fantastic design, great music, delightful secrets, and more. The achievements list is short but meaningful instead of padded – one or two of the achievements here may double your playtime if you care to go for them, and you should. 

Some of you may be skeptical, having played other hacking sim type games and come away disappointed from them. You should be. This is a genre that, frankly, deserves much better in general than it has gotten from developers. Hacknet is, however, different. Hacknet is a game with a power story to tell that will take twists and turns that you do not expect, and resonates with each playthrough no less than it did the first time. 

Even if we were to disregard the story, Hacknet is mechanically incredible. It takes direct inspiration from the command lines of Linux-based operating systems – if you know what 'man' does, try typing it in-game, for just one non-spoiler example – and manages a fantastic level of immersion by removing layers of arbitration between the player and the game. There's no pressing 'w' or 'up' to run here – no running at all, in fact. 

This is one of those indie titles that basically every gamer should buy, play, beat, and complete, if at all possible. Don't miss out on this one.

HackNet isn't just a hacking simulator, it's a living world filled with people from all the different corners of the world connected by internet, world of technology and it's flaws that uses a simple way of mirroring the reality. In this world, you're just a tiny single node in the literal web of billions and even though the world around you feels huge, you can and will change it. But to do that you need to sink down into the corners of this web, sneak around the highest walls, prove youreself worthy and find the truth to the origin of HackNet itself.

  I’ve played a bit longer, and I have more opinions.

The base game is really fun with an exciting storyline. You get to use real UNIX commands such as cat, mv, and cd and I feel like it adds some more realism in the game. You gotta act fast some times because of time pressure (trace). 

The Labyrinths DLC adds a lot to the base game. It adds a whole new story and a lot of new challenges. It's like a whole new game. 

The soundtracks for both the base game, and the DLC, were amazing. I absolutely loved them.

The game is one of my favorite games and I would recommend it to anyone who likes "hacking simulators" and good storylines. Also, get the DLC.

I got this for free (or in a bundle, I don't remember) and I loved it so much I bought the DLC too. This is one of (if not the!) best hacking sim game I've ever played.
